How many received signals does the INS system require?

The heart of the INS is the accelerometer. This device measures an aircraft's acceleration, which is therefore used to calculate velocity and position. An accelerometer can measure acceleration in only two directions, which means more than one is used.

Even though a basic INS system only requires two accelerometers, most aircraft use three. This provides acceleration measurements in all axes. There are two basic types of accelerometers in use today; conventional gyro, and solid-state gyro.

Today, Flight Management Computers (FMC) are used to greatly reduce the error of all systems. An FMC will monitor the information from all navigational systems and determine which values are correct. If a systems information isn't correct it is either reset or disregarded.

A change in the accuracy of a satellites transmissions can be caused by drift. In other words, the orbit path of the satellite has changed for some reason. Drift is a change in the orbit path of a satellite.

The control segment is used to control the satellites. At least once a day various ground stations will receive the information from all of the satellites and send that information to a master control station.

It is here that the information from each of the GPS satellites is analyzed. The master control station will send correction signals back to the satellites if their information is not correct. These signals will recalibrate the satellite's data.

The first segment we will discuss is the space segment. This is a group of satellites that are located in space, orbiting earth. There are a total of 24 satellites, 21 which are active, and 3 for backup.

Near the runway there are two types of signal generators; the localizer and the glide slope. The localizer transmits from approximately 1000 feet from the end of the runway. The localizer transmits two horizontal signals which the plane will use to determine the center of the runway.

It is important to note that basic ILS systems will bring the plane within 200 feet of the runway. At this point the pilot of the aircraft will determine if landing is possible. If not the pilot will perform missed approached procedures and try again.

The Instrument Landing System (ILS) is a system designed to aid a pilot in landing an airplane. This is very helpful when landing conditions are poor. Most ILS systems are accurate to a half mile, meaning visual references are still necessary.

Even though the ILS system assists the pilot in landing, it normally doesn't give an indication of the distance to the end of the runway. Marker beacons are used to indicate distance from the end of the runway.

The first marker beacon the aircraft encounters is the outer marker, it is 5 miles from the end of the runway. When the aircraft passes over the marker a blue light begins flashing on the instrument panel and a buzzer will sound.
As the plane approaches 2/3 of a mile an amber light will begin to flash and a higher pitched buzzer will begin to sound. This means the aircraft is over the middle marker.
Some airports have an inner marker. It is located 1500 feet from the end of the runway. When the aircraft is over this marker a white light flashes. This is an optional beacon.
